title: Criptech, data, and accessible art
introduction: This week's reading was 'Criptech and the Art of Access' by Vanessa Chang and Lindsey Felt, and it changed how I think about disability, technology and art. I worked through three unfamiliar terms from the article, then used them to look more closely at two artists whose practice connects sensors, data and accessibility.
related_work: After reading the article I explored three terms. Criptech art describes artistic practices in which disabled artists use digital and scientific technologies as creative materials and as ways to challenge exclusion. Crip technoscience, from Hamraie and Fritsch, refers to practices through which disabled people critique, adapt and reinvent technologies and environments, recognising disabled people as knowledgeable designers of everyday life. Alt text provides a text equivalent for an image's information or function, communicated by screen readers through speech or braille. I then researched two projects. Itziar Barrio's 2023 exhibition 'did not feel low, was sleeping' at Smack Mellon combines films and sculptures, including robotic sculptures developed from researcher Laura Forlano's smart insulin pump data, the device's alerts and alarms transcribed and annotated with field notes. 'Alt Text as Poetry' by Bojana Coklyat and Finnegan Shannon is a collaborative project that explores image description through poetic approaches, using a workbook and workshops to encourage careful word choice and experimentation.
method: I pinned down each term first, then read the two projects through that lens. For Barrio I focused on how personal medical data becomes material for sculpture; for Coklyat and Shannon I focused on how description becomes a creative practice. The question throughout was the same: whose experience gets included when a technology is designed or an artwork is described.
results_discussion: Working through the terms flipped the usual story. Technology is often presented as something that helps or 'fixes' disabled people, but criptech art and crip technoscience show that disabled people also create, change and question technology, and that access is something people actively build rather than something handed to them. Barrio's work makes the labour of living with and maintaining technology more visible, and it made me ask what a measurement leaves out: a device can record bodily information, but that information never fully explains a person's experience. Because I work with sensors and interactive installations, that is a question I want to carry into my own practice. Coklyat and Shannon showed me that the words chosen to describe an image can communicate its atmosphere as well as its content. For my digital archaeology website, that means writing descriptions that convey both the appearance of an abandoned smartwatch and the sense of decay I want to explore, while still carrying the important visual information clearly.
conclusion_future_work: Both projects push me to look beyond what technology can do technically. Barrio raises questions about the labour behind data, and Coklyat and Shannon show how accessibility can shape artistic expression rather than limit it. Together they make me think more carefully about the people who produce, use and experience my work. My takeaway is that access belongs inside the creative process from the beginning, so I want to design my interactive work with that in mind from the first sketch.
